name: Joseph
bio:
Joseph is the firstborn son of Jacob and Rachel, Jacob's most beloved son, and the central figure of the longest and most dramatic individual story in the whole book of Genesis. His life swings from being favored above his brothers, to being sold into slavery by them, to imprisonment, and finally to becoming Egypt's prime minister — all the while secretly guided by God's providence.

## 👤 Identity and Background: A Beloved but Resented Son

Joseph was born to Jacob in his old age, by his beloved wife Rachel, and so was favored above his brothers — Jacob even made him a coat of many colors, visibly setting him apart (Genesis 37:3). He also had two dreams foretelling that his family would one day bow down to him, and told his brothers about them plainly, deepening their resentment of him (Genesis 37:5-11).

## 📖 Core Story: From the Pit to the Throne

1. **Sold into Slavery**: Jealous, his brothers plotted against him. They first intended to kill him; Reuben talked them into throwing him into a dry pit instead, and Judah proposed selling him to a caravan of Ishmaelites. Joseph was sold into Egypt and became a servant in Potiphar's household (Genesis 37).
2. **Tested in Potiphar's House**: The LORD was with Joseph, and he prospered in everything — until he refused his master's wife's advances and was falsely accused and imprisoned (Genesis 39).
3. **Gifted Even in Prison**: In prison, Joseph accurately interpreted dreams for Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker, but was then forgotten for two years — until Pharaoh himself had troubling dreams, and Joseph was summoned to interpret them (Genesis 40-41).
4. **Prime Minister, Preparing for Famine**: Joseph correctly interpreted Pharaoh's dream of seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine; Pharaoh set him over all Egypt, and his careful storage of grain during the plentiful years allowed Egypt and surrounding nations to survive the famine (Genesis 41).
5. **Reunited with His Brothers**: The famine forced his brothers to come to Egypt to buy grain. Joseph tested them repeatedly to see whether they had truly changed, and was finally convinced by Judah's willingness to take Benjamin's punishment upon himself. Joseph then revealed his identity, wept with his brothers, and brought the whole family to live in Egypt (Genesis 42-46).

## ✨ Key Character and Theological Significance

- **A Model of Faithfulness in Suffering**: Whether enslaved or imprisoned, Joseph consistently refused to sin against God and did his work with full diligence, showing that real faith holds steady in adversity, not just in times of ease.
- **A Witness that God Works All Things Together for Good**: Joseph's words to his brothers summarize the theology of the whole book of Genesis: "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive" (Genesis 50:20) — showing that God can turn human malice into an instrument for accomplishing His good purposes.
- **A Foreshadowing of Christ, the Suffering Servant**: Joseph's story — betrayed by those closest to him, suffering unjustly, yet ultimately saving many from death — is often seen as a foreshadowing of Jesus Christ's own path of being betrayed, suffering, and accomplishing salvation for the world.

Joseph's life tells us that God's providence is often hidden behind what looks like the darkest and most unfair circumstances, and that remaining faithful to God will, in His own time, bring about unexpected blessing and fulfillment.
